why:
phase-456 W9 — the FUTURE-style service client, split out of `rclcpp::Client<S>`, exactly as W2b split `nros::PollSubscription<M>` out of `Subscription<M>` and W5 split `nros::PollService<S>` out of `Service<S>`. Ours-only because of its OWNERSHIP, not its method names: the caller declares it in its own frame, it holds the `RmwServiceClient` in `storage_`, nothing dispatches, and the caller drains the reply itself — through the `Future` `send_request()` hands back, through the blocking `call()`, or through `call_polling()`. Upstream has no such entity: a `rclcpp::Client` belongs to the node, and a reply is taken either through the future `async_send_request` returns or through a callback given to it.

WHY IT WAS SPLIT, and the reason is the same one measured for subscriptions and then for services. One class served both owners behind a `callback_mode_` flag, and `storage_` is filled only on the future-style path — the arena owns the client on the other one. So `wait_for_service()` on a callback-mode object handed `NROS_SERVICE_CLIENT_SIZE` value-initialized zero bytes to `nros_cpp_service_client_wait_for_service`, whose own doc comment says `storage` must be "a valid initialized future-style service client", with `initialized_` true and nothing on the path checking. `service_is_ready()`, `server_available()`, `send_request()`, `call()` and `call_polling()` were all reachable the same way. Splitting the types makes those calls unwritable rather than merely discouraged.

AND IT UNBLOCKED THE ALIAS. W3 recorded the blocker and W6 costed it: `create_client<S>(name, qos)` with no handler returned `Client<S>::SharedPtr` and existed to be `->send_request()`'d, so one alias could not be both an arena handle and a pointer to a caller-owned object. It returns `nros::Owned<PollClient<S>>` now, and `Client<S>::SharedPtr` is `nros::ClientHandle<S>` — see `cpp:ClientHandle`.
